title: Zeus — Echoes in later ages

Long after its gods lost worshippers, Zeus kept working — in Renaissance painting, in Romantic poetry, in modern film. Each age found its own anxieties reflected in the old story. Myths survive by being reusable. Zeus proved endlessly reusable. A fourth sub-question examines the moral the myth was meant to teach its first hearers. Related entries in this archive: Maya ballgame and Wendigo.

Myths are carried by persons — gods who are larger than human, heroes who are almost, monsters who embody what must be faced. In Ares, each figure plays a role that reveals what the culture feared, honored, and desired. Viewed through a cultural lens, Ares is examined as a people's self-portrait — the values and fears it encodes.

The figures of Ares outlive their religion: they become metaphors the whole world now uses. A second sub-question concerns the historical kernel: what real events or places might stand behind Ares. Related entries in this archive: Ganesha and Tuatha De Danann.

Myths answer questions science had not yet asked: why the seasons turn, why suffering exists, why kings rule. Viewed through a narrative lens, Demeter is examined as story — its plot, its pacing, and the moments that make it unforgettable.

To ask what Demeter explains is to recover the curiosity that made it. A fourth sub-question examines the moral the myth was meant to teach its first hearers. Related entries in this archive: Hades and Pegasus.

title: Odysseus — Ritual and worship
summary: Odysseus, hero of the Odyssey, took ten years to return home from Troy. This study follows the myth into temples and festivals.
body:
Odysseus, hero of the Odyssey, took ten years to return home from Troy. His cunning — the Trojan Horse, the blinding of Polyphemus — defines him.

Myths were not entertainment; they were scripts for ritual. Odysseus was enacted in festivals, sacrifices, and mysteries that bound communities together and aligned human time with cosmic time. Viewed through a cultural lens, Odysseus is examined as a people's self-portrait — the values and fears it encodes.

Where the myth was performed, it was believed with the body, not just the mind. A fourth sub-question examines the moral the myth was meant to teach its first hearers. Related entries in this archive: Heimdall and Coyote the trickster.

title: Achilles — The tale itself
summary: Achilles, the Iliad's greatest warrior, chose a short glorious life over long obscurity. This study tells the myth straight and complete.
body:
Achilles, the Iliad's greatest warrior, chose a short glorious life over long obscurity. His heel was his only vulnerability, giving us the 'Achilles heel.'

Every myth deserves to be heard as story first. Achilles unfolds with its own logic — characters acting from motives the myth takes for granted, events following one another with dreamlike necessity. To know Achilles is to be able to tell it. Viewed through a symbolic lens, Achilles is read for its images — what each figure and object stands for beneath the plot.

The story is the data. All interpretation comes after, and must answer to the tale as told. A third sub-question asks how Achilles was visualized — in vase painting, sculpture, or temple relief. Related entries in this archive: Raijin and Fujin and Perseus.
key_points: The full narrative of Achilles preserved.

title: Trojan War — Comparative mythology
summary: The Trojan War was fought over Helen, lasting ten years and ending with the wooden horse. This study sets the myth beside its cousins worldwide.
body:
The Trojan War was fought over Helen, lasting ten years and ending with the wooden horse. Homer's Iliad covers only a few weeks of its final year.

Floods, tricksters, dying gods, world trees — the same patterns recur across continents. Setting Trojan War beside its parallels tests whether the pattern is human nature, cultural diffusion, or coincidence. Viewed through a symbolic lens, Trojan War is read for its images — what each figure and object stands for beneath the plot.

Comparison honors Trojan War by taking it seriously as one answer among many. A fourth sub-question examines the moral the myth was meant to teach its first hearers. Related entries in this archive: Bifrost and Ziggurats.
key_points: Trojan War compared with world parallels.

title: Prometheus — Variants across tellings
summary: Prometheus stole fire for humanity and was chained to a rock where an eagle ate his liver daily. This study compares how different sources tell the tale.
body:
Prometheus stole fire for humanity and was chained to a rock where an eagle ate his liver daily. He embodies the suffering benefactor of mankind.

No myth has one true version. Prometheus survives in competing tellings — poets, priests, and painters each shaping it to their purpose. The variants disagree, and the disagreements are themselves revealing. Viewed through a narrative lens, Prometheus is examined as story — its plot, its pacing, and the moments that make it unforgettable.

The 'real' Prometheus is the whole cloud of versions, not any single text. A second sub-question concerns the historical kernel: what real events or places might stand behind Prometheus. Related entries in this archive: Valhalla and Enuma Elish.

title: Icarus — What the myth explains
summary: Icarus flew too close to the sun on wax wings made by his father Daedalus. This study reads the myth as an answer to a question.
body:
Icarus flew too close to the sun on wax wings made by his father Daedalus. His fall warns against hubris.

Myths answer questions science had not yet asked: why the seasons turn, why suffering exists, why kings rule. Icarus encodes its culture's answers in narrative form — explanations you can remember because they move you. Viewed through a contemporary-relevance lens, Icarus is brought into the present, where its patterns still appear in new clothes.

To ask what Icarus explains is to recover the curiosity that made it. A second sub-question concerns the historical kernel: what real events or places might stand behind Icarus. Related entries in this archive: The Furies and Shiva.
